+# Linux Job Worker Service
+
+## Scope
+
+A service that runs arbitrary Linux processes on behalf of clients. The system consists of three components:
+
+1. **Worker library:** Go library that provides an interface for start/stop/query status for jobs (Linux process).
+2. **API server:** gRPC API that wraps that Worker Library and provides the same interface but exposed over the network.
+3. **Client:** CLI client for connecting to the API and sending requests. Provides the same interface as the other components.
+
+### Not in scope
+* Architecting for scale
+* High performance
+* High availability
+* Persistence between server restarts
+
+## Design
+
+### Worker Library
+
+Each job is represented by a `Job` struct holding the process state, a unique id, and an output buffer in the form of a Go channel. 
+
+The library exposes four operations: **Start**, **Stop**, **Status**.
+
+```go
+type JobState int
+
+const (
+  JobRunning JobState = iota
+  JobStopped
+)
+
+type Job struct {
+  id int64
+  state JobState
+  output chan string
+}
+
+type Jobs interface {
+  Start(string) (Job, error)
+  Stop(int64) error
+  Status(int64) error
+}
+```
+
+#### Process management
+`Start()` spawns a Linux process via `cmd.Start()` within `os/exec`. The `os/exec` package exposes methods for receiving pipes of StdOut and StdErr that we can use to send updates to the `Job` channel in a background goroutine. This will prevent blocking on process start. The channel will also allow for non-blocking behaviour in the consumer of this API, as they can just loop over the `range` of the channel when requested to stream the data. An option to record the exit code of the Linux process is also possible here, and we could record that in our struct for any clients that care when they request status of their Job.
+
+### gRPC API
+
+The service definition:
+
+```protobuf
+syntax = "proto3";
+package jobs;
+
+service JobsAPI {
+  rpc Start(StartRequest)           returns (StartResponse);
+  rpc Stop(StopRequest)             returns (StopResponse);
+  rpc Status(StatusRequest)         returns (StatusResponse);
+  rpc StreamOutput(OutputRequest)   returns (stream OutputResponse);
+}
+```
+
+#### Streaming output
+
+We acheive data streaming by using a server-side streaming RPC with the keyword `stream`. We have a subtle problem here though, as we have a channel for streaming updates from the Linux process, and an RPC for streaming updates to the API client, but Go channels only work on a single-consumer basis and channel state is not retained after messages are received. This poses a problem for concurrent readers of the output and when getting caught-up on the earlier process output.
+
+1. **Concurrent readers problem:** When a process is started, we will need to spawn a background goroutine to receieve the channel updates and broadcast the output to "registered listeners". When a client calls in to start streaming output they will be "registered" and receive data off of their own discrete output channel stream that is being piped in from the original `Job` "source channel" stream. This system will fan out the output to all "registered" client channels as updates come in.
comment.body: 👍 Updated the streaming output design to allow for slow/flaky clients that don't get terminated and don't block anyone else.

+```

+#### Streaming output
+
+We acheive data streaming by using a server-side streaming RPC with the keyword `stream`. We have a subtle problem here though, as we have a channel for streaming updates from the Linux process, and an RPC for streaming updates to the API client, but Go channels only work on a single-consumer basis and channel state is not retained after messages are received. This poses a problem for concurrent readers of the output and when getting caught-up on the earlier process output.
+
+1. **Concurrent readers problem:** When a process is started, we will need to spawn a background goroutine to receieve the channel updates and broadcast the output to "registered listeners". comment.body: 👍 Updated the design to emphasize not sending massive blobs of history over the wire and not retain copies of the Job history longer than needed. The history will be copied (efficiently) over when someone new subscribes, but as the Subscriber chews through it and processes, it will discard its copy of the history since it's useless at that point.

comment.body:
> The solution is to put a small timeout for registered channels in the fanout process and buffer the client channels as well for some breathing room. If a client channel times out during a send, a simple procedure could be to close the channel with a sentinel message indicating they timed out and will be receiving no more output.

For this challenge we are looking for a solution that is not susceptible to deadlocks and provides all output to clients, no matter how fast or slow they can consume it. With that in mind the library or server closing the client is not an acceptable solution.
